groups.title: Questions 21-26.
groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, or C

questions.text: Eleanor thinks eyewitnesses are believed when

options.text: they are respected members of the community.
they make their statements with confidence.
they use sophisticated language in their accounts.

questions.text: What concerns Duckie, Eleanor, and Jamie about the texts they have read so far?

options.text: No clear conclusions are reached.
The studies involved comparatively few people.
Some of the data were gathered some time ago.

questions.text: They agree that the most significant factor affecting eyewitness reliability is

options.text: how good the lighting is.
how long the event lasts.
how far away the witness is.
fail to compare the photos with their memory of the event.
are not properly briefed about the procedure.
they are keen for the case to be concluded.

questions.text: They agree that the term ‘naive observer’ means a person who

options.text: has no experience of a police investigation.
did not realize they were witnessing a crime.
was not present at the incident.

questions.text: They have learned that witnesses are reluctant to change their opinions because

options.text: they do not want to appear foolish.
they fear the legal consequences.
they are keen for the case to be concluded.

groups.title: Questions 27-30.
groups.instruction: What problem may there be with child witnesses at each of the following stages of an interview?

options.text: Frightened by the unfamiliar environment
Influenced by the interviewer Duckie
Not understanding the difference between truth and lies
Unwillingness to say they don’t know
Confused by the terminology
Distrust of the interviewer

transcript.text: Now turn to Section 3 on page 5.
Section 3
You will hear two law students called Eleanor and Jamie discussing their work on whether
the evidence given by people who witness crimes is reliable.
First, you have some time to look at questions 21-26 on page 5.
You will hear two law students called Eleanor and Jamie discussing their work on whether
the evidence given by people who witness crimes is reliable.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 21-26.
Eleanor: Hi Jamie, I've just been reading this book about eyewitness testimonies.
It really goes into how much we can actually rely on what the people who witness crimes
actually say and what things influence eyewitness reliability.
Jamie: Oh, I've read a couple of case studies on that too.
Can we compare notes?
Eleanor: Good idea.
It's fascinating to learn that eyewitness identification is such compelling evidence
in both civil and criminal trials.
Jamie: You mean if a witness says something generally they're believed?
Eleanor: And reading between the lines, I'd say that when a witness gives evidence in a very
self-assured way, everyone takes them at their word, whether they're a doctor who speaks
with an assumed authority or the average person in the street, it doesn't seem to matter
as much as their manner.
Jamie: Right.
So is that textbook worth reading?
Eleanor: Yes.
It's a good book, divided into user-friendly sections.
It refers to case studies and the conclusions are clearly underlined, but actually some
of the cases are more than 10 years old now.
Jamie: Well, it's the same problem with the survey reports our tutor gave us, but at least they
draw on a representative sample.
Eleanor: That's good.
All the books point out that eyewitness statements are very often unreliable.
Eleanor:But there can be good reasons for that, like an incident may happen at night in the dark.
Jamie: Or it happens some way away, but it's the fact that it can happen in just a split second
that makes the witnesses account so unreliable.
Eleanor: That point's made very strongly in what I've read too.
Jamie: Yeah.
Eleanor：Have you read anything about photo identifications?
Jamie: Yes.
About the procedure and the reliability of witnesses looking at photos of different people
and picking out the suspect.
The case studies all clearly show how easy it is to sway a witness's choice of photo even
just by the flicker of an eye.
But steps have been taken now to avoid this happening.
Eleanor: And are the witnesses told exactly what they have to do?
Jamie: Mostly.
But the trouble is, most people focus on the photos and choose the most likely suspect
from the bunch and forget about the actual incident and who they saw at the time.
Eleanor: Did I read something about a naive observer?
Do you know what that is?
Is it a witness who's never been in a court before?
Jamie: Oh.
I understood it to mean someone who's had nothing to do with the event.
And they're asked to look at the photos and pick out the potential suspect.
Eleanor: That figures.
Then they can see if the photos are a good set and make sure one person doesn't stand
out.
Jamie: Another thing I read was that witnesses don't like to change their minds once they've made
a particular statement.
I thought people might worry about the fact that they told a lie in court and think they
might be punished in some way.
But it's simply that they're afraid of seeming unintelligent or lightweight.
Eleanor: Yeah.
People are reluctant to lose face.
Imagine if a case had been going on for weeks and you suddenly realised you'd got something
wrong right at the beginning.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27-30
on page 6.
Now listen and answer questions 27-30.
Eleanor: Changing the topic slightly, can I just check with you what you've understood about the
problems of interviewing child witnesses when they've witnessed, for example, robbery?
Jamie: Yes.
Did you get the handout about the stages that should be followed when children are interviewed?
Eleanor：Yes.
The rapport stage, when a relationship between the child and the interviewer is built
up, seems to be crucial.
Jamie：But many children fail to say anything that provides any real information.
It must be hard for them not to feel a bit scared about being in a formal setting like
a court building.
Still, it's a good lead-in to open-ended questions where the interviewer carefully
sticks to their prepared questions in order to remain neutral.
Eleanor: I can see the point of that, but the handout discusses the issue of children simply not understanding
the specialist language used, so the whole interview just gets more puzzling for them.
I think the stage called closed questions is easier for children to handle.
They just have to answer yes or no.
Jamie：But everything's not so clear cut in a child's world.
And abstract concepts such as honesty haven't been fully grasped by young children.
Eleanor：You mean they make things up?
Jamie：Apparently.
And in the final stage, closure, where the interviewer has to check anything that hasn't
been made clear to them by repeating previous questions, children often become suspicious
of the questioner.
Eleanor：It must require lots of training to be able to interview children successfully.
Jamie：Yes, I think.
There is the end of section three.
You now have half a minute to check your answers.
